passages.t: Ephraim's anger, and a soft answer
passages.happening:
The men of Ephraim come to Gideon angry. “Why have you done this to us? Why did you fail to call us when you went to fight against Midian?” (verse 1). They argue with him fiercely.

Gideon answers with praise. “Now what have I accomplished compared to you? Are not the gleanings of Ephraim better than the grape harvest of Abiezer?” (verse 2). God gave the two princes of Midian into their hands, he says, and what could he do compared with that? (verse 3).

When he says this, their anger cools.
passages.hearers:
Ephraim was one of the largest tribes, in the hills at the center of the land, and it seems to have seen itself as the natural leader of the northern tribes. It was offended to be called in late, only to guard the fords.

Gideon answers with a saying from the grape harvest. The gleanings are the grapes left on the vines after the main picking. Abiezer was Gideon's own clan. He is saying that Ephraim's leftovers, the capture of Oreb and Zeeb, are worth more than his clan's whole harvest. It is flattery, and it works.

It is worth setting this beside chapter 12, where the men of Ephraim come with the same complaint to another judge, Jephthah. He will not answer softly, and many will die.
passages.later:
A proverb says what Gideon did: “A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger” (Proverbs 15:1).

Ephraim stayed the leading tribe of the north. After the kingdom divided, the prophets often called the whole northern kingdom by its name: “Aram was in league with Ephraim” (Isaiah 7:2).
passages.asks: Gideon turned away a quarrel with a few generous words. Ask whether there is an angry person in your life whom a gentle answer might quiet. And ask whether your own pride ever makes you, like Ephraim, more upset about being left out than glad that the work was done.

passages.happening:
Gideon and his three hundred cross the Jordan, ‘exhausted yet still in pursuit’ (verse 4). He asks the town of Succoth for bread for his men, but its leaders mock him. “Are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna already in your possession, that we should give bread to your army?” (verse 6). Gideon swears that when he returns he will tear their flesh with thorns and briers. The town of Penuel refuses too, and he swears he will pull down its tower (verses 7-9).

He catches up with the two kings of Midian and their army at Karkor, takes them by surprise, and captures both kings (verses 10-12).

On the way back he seizes a young man of Succoth, who writes down the names of the town's seventy-seven leaders and elders (verse 14). Gideon punishes the elders of Succoth with thorns and briers, pulls down the tower of Penuel, and kills the men of the city (verses 16-17).

Then he asks the two kings about the men they killed at Tabor. They answer that the men looked like him, like the sons of a king. “They were my brothers,” Gideon replied, “the sons of my mother!” (verse 19). He tells his oldest son, Jether, to kill them, but the boy is afraid. So Gideon kills them himself and takes the crescent ornaments from their camels' necks (verses 20-21).
passages.hearers:
Succoth and Penuel were towns of Israel east of the Jordan, near the river Jabbok. Both appear in the story of Jacob, who built shelters at Succoth and wrestled with God at Penuel.

Their refusal was probably caution more than treachery. If Gideon failed, the Midianites would take revenge on any town that had helped him. Their fear was understandable. But they also sneered at a hungry army that was fighting for them.

The note that a young man of Succoth could write down seventy-seven names is a small glimpse of writing in early Israel. Alphabetic writing was in use in Canaan by this time, and short inscriptions from the early Iron Age have been found in the region.

The tone of the story has changed. In chapter 7 every step began with God. Here God is hardly mentioned. Gideon's words become threats and oaths, and his acts are driven by his own grievances. The men he punishes and kills are not Midianites but Israelites.

The killing of the two kings is told as revenge for Gideon's brothers, who had been killed at Tabor, an event the text does not otherwise describe. In the ancient world, avenging murdered kin was counted a duty. Asking a boy to kill captured kings was meant to shame them, and they ask instead for a warrior's death. None of this is held up as a pattern. It shows how a deliverer begins to fight his own wars.
passages.later:
Jacob's story gave these towns their names: “So Jacob named the place Peniel, saying, ‘Indeed, I have seen God face to face, and yet my life was spared’” (Genesis 32:30), and “Jacob went on to Succoth, where he built a house for himself and shelters for his livestock” (Genesis 33:17).

The law later took vengeance out of human hands: “Vengeance is Mine; I will repay” (Deuteronomy 32:35). Paul quotes it to the church (Romans 12:19).
passages.hard:
Was Gideon right to punish Succoth and Penuel?

Gideon punished the elders of Succoth with thorns and briers and killed the men of Penuel, fellow Israelites who had refused him food.

Some readers see rough wartime justice. In a crisis, those towns refused to help the deliverer God had sent, and so in effect sided with the enemy.

Others read the story as quietly critical of Gideon. God is absent from these scenes. The violence falls on Israelites, not on oppressors. And it fits the book's pattern of judges who grow worse. The towns' fear was understandable too, since Gideon's success was not yet certain.

Many readers conclude that the narrator is showing, without saying it outright, how a deliverer can become an oppressor of his own people. These notes do not settle the question, but they note how much has changed since the night of the three hundred horns.
passages.asks: Gideon was tired, insulted and grieving his brothers, and he let those things lead. Ask what you do when you are exhausted and someone sneers at you. And ask whether there is a grievance you have carried so long that it has become the reason for what you do.

passages.t: ‘The LORD shall rule over you’, and the gold ephod
passages.happening:
The Israelites ask Gideon to rule over them, and his son and grandson after him, because he saved them from Midian (verse 22).

Gideon refuses. “I will not rule over you, nor will my son. The LORD shall rule over you” (verse 23).

Then he makes a request. Each man is to give him a gold earring from the plunder. They spread out a garment and throw the earrings on it. The gold weighs 1,700 shekels, besides the ornaments, the purple robes of the kings of Midian, and the chains from their camels' necks (verses 24-26).

“From all this Gideon made an ephod, which he placed in Ophrah, his hometown. But soon all Israel prostituted themselves by worshiping it there, and it became a snare to Gideon and his household” (verse 27).

Midian never rises again, and the land has rest for forty years in Gideon's days (verse 28).
passages.hearers:
Gideon's refusal is the high point of his story. In a few words he states Israel's true faith: God himself is Israel's king. No man should take that place.

Then the story undercuts his words at once. He asks for gold. The earrings, crescent ornaments and pendants were the kind of wealth desert peoples wore on their bodies. The 1,700 shekels of gold weighed roughly forty pounds, about nineteen kilograms.

An ephod was a garment worn by priests, and the high priest's ephod was used in seeking God's guidance. Gideon's gold ephod may have been a garment of that kind, or it may have been an object of worship of some other kind. Either way, it became a center of worship in his hometown, a rival to the place God had appointed. The note on the ephod in the hard question below says more.

The phrase ‘prostituted themselves’ is the book's strongest word for unfaithfulness to God, like a husband or wife breaking a marriage. It comes here while Gideon is still alive.

The word ‘snare’ has been heard before. At Bochim God warned that the gods of the nations would be a snare to Israel (2:3). Now the snare is made by Israel's own judge, out of the gold of his victory.
passages.later:
The law said that even a king must not gather gold for himself: “He must not take many wives for himself, lest his heart go astray. He must not accumulate for himself large amounts of silver and gold” (Deuteronomy 17:17). Gideon refused the crown, and the next verses show that he did both.

Elsewhere the ephod is the priest's means of asking God's guidance: when David needed to know what to do, “he said to Abiathar the priest, ‘Bring the ephod’” (1 Samuel 23:9).
passages.hard:
How could the man who tore down Baal's altar end by making something Israel worshiped?

The text does not tell what Gideon meant by the ephod. Some think he intended a memorial of the victory. Others think he meant it as a way of seeking God's guidance, like the priest's ephod. Whatever he intended, the result is plain: ‘all Israel prostituted themselves by worshiping it there, and it became a snare to Gideon and his household’.

That is the lesson the book draws. Idolatry can grow out of a victory and out of good intentions. A thing made in God's name, from the gifts of a grateful people, became a rival to God himself. The judge who began by pulling down his father's idol ends by setting up his own.

The same chapter holds Gideon's finest words and his gravest failure side by side. The book does not explain away either one.
passages.asks: Gideon said ‘The LORD shall rule over you’, and then gathered gold. Ask where your words about God's rule and your use of money or power do not match. And ask whether anything you made in God's name, a ministry, a habit, a good work, has begun to take his place.

passages.happening:
Gideon goes home and settles down. He has seventy sons, because he has many wives (verses 29-30). His concubine in Shechem also bears him a son, and he names him Abimelech (verse 31). Gideon dies at a good old age and is buried in his father's tomb at Ophrah (verse 32).

“And as soon as Gideon was dead, the Israelites turned and prostituted themselves with the Baals, and they set up Baal-berith as their god” (verse 33). “The Israelites failed to remember the LORD their God who had delivered them from the hands of all their enemies on every side” (verse 34). Nor do they show kindness to Gideon's family for all the good he had done (verse 35).
passages.hearers:
Many wives and a concubine, a secondary wife of lower standing, were marks of kings and wealthy men in the ancient world. Gideon had said he would not rule. He lived like a ruler.

The name he gave his son says the same. Abimelech joins the Hebrew words for father and king, and it says that the boy's father is a king. The next chapter shows what that son made of it.

As soon as Gideon dies, the wheel of chapter 2 turns again. Israel goes back to Baal, and this time to a Baal with a telling name. Baal-berith means Baal of the covenant, a god worshiped at Shechem. Israel belonged to the LORD by covenant, and it gave its covenant loyalty to Baal.

Verse 34 echoes the book's opening diagnosis, the generation that did not know the LORD. Israel ‘failed to remember’ him. Forgetting God and forgetting those who served them go together in verse 35.

Notice too what is missing. After Gideon the land is never again said to have rest.
passages.later: A psalm sums up this whole history of forgetting in one line: “They forgot God their Savior, who did great things in Egypt” (Psalm 106:21).
passages.asks: Israel forgot God the day its leader died. Ask whether your faith depends on a person, a pastor, a parent or a friend, more than on God himself. And ask what it would take for your faith to outlast the people who first helped you to it.
